Diagnosis: Severe Dengue Fever (Grade I) with COVID-19

The patient is a 39-year-old Asian male. He came to the emergency room with high fever, headache, tiredness, muscle pain, pain in the upper right belly area, vomiting, and loose stools. During the physical exam, he showed signs of not having enough fluids in his body. He also had pain when the doctor pressed on his upper right belly area. Blood tests showed his blood was thicker than normal (19% increase). His liver function tests were also higher than normal. One test for dengue fever (NS1) came back negative. The patient was kept separate from other patients in the COVID-19 unit. His diagnosis was severe dengue fever (Grade I) along with COVID-19. His blood thickness only went up a small amount. He was treated with drinking fluids by mouth. On day 5 of his illness, he developed a dry cough and sore throat. A chest X-ray was done and showed no problems.

During his hospital stay, the care team checked him every day for warning signs of dengue fever getting worse. This included watching his blood thickness levels. His stay in the hospital went smoothly without any problems. He was sent home after staying in isolation for the required 14 days.

Follow-up:
The patient should see his regular doctor or an infection specialist as told in his discharge papers. He was given instructions about his medications to take at home. He was also told to keep watching for any new symptoms or warning signs.

Reason for Admission: Fever and very low white blood cell count

Diagnosis: Skin cancer that has spread to other parts of the body with low Vitamin B6 levels

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 51-year-old woman with blood cancer that came back after treatment. She had received donor stem cells four years earlier. She came to the hospital with fever and very low white blood cell count. Blood tests showed a normal total white blood cell count. However, only 2% were infection-fighting cells. The rest were 84% immune cells and 14% other white blood cells. Red blood cells were normal. The patient had a history of her body attacking itself after the transplant. This affected her skin and caused skin cancer. Her medicines to lower her immune system were stopped two months earlier because of the skin cancer. Blood tests found bacteria called micrococcus. Her fever went away after taking an antibiotic called vancomycin.

A test of the patient's bone marrow showed very few cells. A sample taken from a neck lymph node showed cancer cells. This meant the skin cancer had spread. The patient was given medicine to boost white blood cell growth. This did not help raise her white blood cell count. After taking 150 mg of Vitamin B6 each day, her B6 levels became normal. Her white blood cell count also returned to normal. The swollen lymph nodes in her neck went away completely. Imaging scans showed no signs of cancer in that area.

The patient's medicines were changed during her hospital stay. Three medicines were stopped: valganciclovir, voriconazole, and Soriatane (acitretin). Two new medicines were started to prevent infections: fluconazole and acyclovir. The patient left the hospital in stable condition.

Instructions at Discharge:

The patient was told to see her cancer doctor for ongoing care of her skin cancer that has spread. She was told to keep taking Vitamin B6 every day. She was also told to stay away from people who are sick. The patient was given an appointment to see her regular doctor in three to four weeks.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 55-year-old man with a history of polycythemia vera, a blood disorder where the body makes too many red blood cells. He came to our hospital with trouble breathing, chest pain, low blood cell counts, and fluid buildup around his heart and lungs. His symptoms started 6 weeks after gallbladder removal surgery at another hospital. During that time, he had nausea and vomiting. Doctors then found a sore in his small intestine and damage to his food pipe.

When the patient arrived, doctors drained the fluid from around his lungs and heart to help him feel better. Tests ruled out infection, immune system problems, and heart disease as causes of the fluid buildup. More tests, including a bone marrow sample and gene testing, showed the patient had acute myeloid leukemia, a type of blood cancer. The cancer cells had several gene changes, including extra copies of chromosomes 8, 9, and 21. The cells also had a gene change called JAK2 V617F.

Lab tests on the fluid from around the lungs and heart showed irritated cells and signs of swelling but no cancer cells. Special cell testing showed that most of the cells in the fluid, about 70 percent, looked like basophils, a type of white blood cell. A second fluid sample from the lungs showed the same gene changes found in the bone marrow. This proved the fluid buildup was caused by the leukemia.

The patient received supportive care, including extra oxygen, and started cancer treatment for acute myeloid leukemia. During his hospital stay, the care team watched him closely and treated his symptoms. The patient had a difficult hospital stay but got better over time. He was sent home with plans to see his main doctors often.

The 17-year-old male patient came to the bone doctor at The General Hospital of Jinan Military Commanding Region (Jinan, China). The patient had mild right wrist pain for about two months. During the exam, the doctor found swelling, mild pain when touched, and warmth at the end of the lower arm bone near the wrist. The doctor felt a hard lump with an uneven surface (size, 3×2 cm) on the back of the wrist area. The patient could not move the wrist as well as normal. X-rays showed the bone looked cloudy in some areas and had holes in other areas. The bone also showed signs of irritation in the lower arm bone near the wrist. A special scan called MRI showed a growth that had spread into nearby soft tissue. A bone scan showed the problem area was picking up more of the scanning material than normal.

The patient was found to have bone cancer after doctors took a small sample with a needle and looked at it under a microscope. After two rounds of cancer-fighting drugs (cisplatin, adriamycin, and ifosfamide), the pain got better and the lump got smaller. The patient could also move the wrist normally again. Then, the patient had surgery to remove the tumor in one piece. Doctors rebuilt the area using a bone from the lower leg to save the wrist joint. The smaller arm bone and the joints near the wrist were saved. The leg bone was attached to the arm bone with two metal plates. Then the wound was closed. A long arm cast was put on to hold the wrist in a good position. Tests on the removed tissue showed no cancer cells at the edges of the removed piece or in other parts of the growth.

The patient received more cancer-fighting drugs using the same medicines and amounts as before surgery. This treatment was finished after six rounds. The patient started gentle movement exercises after the arm was protected by the cast for 12 weeks. Six months after surgery, X-rays showed the transplanted leg bone had joined well with the arm bone. The exam showed the patient could bend the wrist back to 90 degrees and bend the palm down to 45 degrees. One month after surgery, there were no signs of wrist problems, looseness, cancer spread, or cancer coming back. The patient is still being checked regularly.

The patient left the hospital in stable condition. The patient received instructions for home care. These included how to take care of the surgery wound and how to do daily activities. Admission Date:
Discharge Date:

History of Present Illness:
The patient is a 52-year-old man who was healthy before this illness. He came to the hospital with a dry cough that had lasted one and a half years. He also coughed up small amounts of blood from time to time. He had a mild fever off and on during this time. When he did cough up mucus, it was small amounts and clear. The fever was low, up to 100 degrees, and came and went without a pattern.

The patient looked healthy and well-fed. His fingers were normal and he had no swollen glands. His lungs sounded mostly normal. However, the upper left part of his chest sounded dull when tapped. Breath sounds were also quieter in that area. His windpipe was in the normal position. His heart, brain, nervous system, and belly all seemed normal.

Diagnostic Evaluation:
Most blood tests came back normal. However, the patient had mild low blood count and signs of swelling in the body. A test for HIV was negative. Two samples of coughed-up mucus did not show TB germs. A chest X-ray showed a cloudy area in the upper left lung. The lung tissue had pulled upward and the left side of the breathing muscle was raised. A detailed scan of the chest showed the upper left lung had partly collapsed and hardened. There were also small calcium spots in that area.

Fiberoptic Bronchoscopy:
The patient had a test where a thin tube with a camera was put into his lungs. This showed red, swollen tissue in the left upper lung. There was also a round growth partly blocking the airway to that part of the lung. A small piece of the growth was removed to test. White, cheese-like material came out of it. Fluid washed from the lungs was tested for germs. No germs showed up right away in the fluid. But the tissue sample showed signs of TB infection. Mucus coughed up after the test did show TB germs. After three weeks, TB germs grew from the lung fluid sample.

Management:
After looking at all test results, the patient was started on TB medicine. He was given a standard treatment plan through a program that watches patients take their medicine. He also took a steroid medicine by mouth. After three months of treatment, another camera test showed the blocked airway was now mostly open. There was still some narrowing.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Tuberculosis

Disposition:
The patient left the hospital in stable condition. He was taught how to take care of himself with TB. This included when to take his medicine and why it is important to take every dose. He also learned how to cover his cough and protect others in public. A follow-up visit was set up with his regular doctor.

None.

Patient: 64-year-old white female with a history of weight loss surgery called gastric bypass, high blood pressure, and bipolar disorder.

Hospital Course:

The patient slowly got better during her hospital stay. She was given a similar calming medicine called clonazepam because it stays in the body longer. She became awake and knew her name, where she was, and the date. The patient could not walk on her own. She needed a wheelchair and help moving from place to place. After 29 days in the hospital, she was sent to a nursing facility for physical therapy.

Follow-up Plan:

The patient will keep taking copper and clonazepam after leaving the hospital. She will have more tests to find out why her vitamin B12 is high and what the growth near her small intestine is. She has appointments set up with her regular doctor and other specialists.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: Female, 46 years old. The patient has Gilbert syndrome, a condition that affects how the liver processes a substance called bilirubin. The patient had surgery to replace the mitral valve in the heart.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital for heart valve surgery. The mitral valve had become too narrow and stiff, making it hard for blood to flow through. Blood tests before surgery showed high bilirubin levels, which confirmed Gilbert syndrome. A heart ultrasound showed some blood was leaking backward through another heart valve called the tricuspid valve. The test also showed higher than normal pressure in the lungs and the right side of the heart was not pumping quite as well as it should. The left side of the heart was pumping normally at 65 percent.

During surgery, the patient received medicine to help with relaxation and sleep. Pain medicine was also given through a needle in the lower back. The old mitral valve was removed and replaced with a mechanical valve. A heart-lung machine pumped blood through the body during surgery for 98 minutes. After surgery, medicines helped the heart pump well again. Pain was controlled with medicine given through the IV and pain shots as needed.

The patient was watched closely for problems after surgery. A heart ultrasound after surgery showed the right side of the heart was still slightly weak. Some blood was still leaking through the tricuspid valve. Blood flow through the liver was measured before and after surgery and stayed about the same. The breathing tube was removed 4 hours after surgery. The patient was able to eat and drink 2 hours after that. The patient stayed in the intensive care unit for 5 days. The total hospital stay was 8 days. Then the patient went home.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Severe narrowing of the mitral valve in the heart, which required surgery to replace the valve.

Discharge Medications:
None listed.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should see the doctor for follow-up visits as scheduled. No other specific instructions were given.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 75-year-old man who came to the hospital with pain in the upper belly area. Blood tests showed problems with how the liver was working. Scans showed that the tubes that carry bile from the liver were swollen and thickened. A special test using a small camera found blockages in the bile tubes. Doctors found that the patient had bile duct cancer near the liver. The patient had surgery to remove the left side of the liver, a small part called the caudate lobe, the bile tube outside the liver, and to reconnect the bile system. The patient left the hospital 23 days after surgery and was doing well.

Follow-up:
Two years and 9 months after the first surgery, a scan showed the cancer had spread to another part of the liver. The patient had surgery to remove a small part of the liver called segment 8. During that surgery, doctors found another tumor in the liver. Doctors removed both tumors, which turned out to be a different type of slow-growing cancer called NET G2. Five years and 4 months after the first surgery, four more liver tumors were found. The patient started getting monthly shots of medicine called octreotide LAR, then switched to another shot called lanreotide. Six years and 3 months after the first surgery, the patient had a third liver surgery. Doctors found seven tumors that were the same NET G2 cancer type. In the fourth surgery, no new tumors were found. The patient left the hospital in stable condition.

Medical Management:
Seven months after the third liver surgery, a check-up showed four liver tumors. The patient took a pill called everolimus for 6 months. All the tumors got smaller. However, the patient had to stop taking this medicine because of side effects.

Clinical Diagnosis:
The patient was found to have bile duct cancer near the liver based on test results, scans, and tissue samples. Later, the cancer spread to other parts of the liver. These new tumors were a different type called NET G2. The patient had several surgeries to remove the tumors and took everolimus medicine. The patient left the hospital in stable condition after each surgery. Follow-up visits showed no new cancer growth.

Impressions:
This patient had bile duct cancer near the liver and later developed a different type of slow-growing cancer called NET G2 that spread within the liver. The patient has had several surgeries and took everolimus medicine. Follow-up visits show no new cancer growth.

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the hospital with swelling in the legs and protein in the urine. A kidney tissue sample showed a disease called amyloidosis. This disease happens when an abnormal protein builds up in the body. Treatment included chemotherapy drugs called melphalan and dexamethasone. The patient also had a transplant using their own stem cells. Sadly, the treatment did not work well enough. The protein levels in the blood stayed high. The patient also kept losing large amounts of protein through urine. Nine months later, the patient had surgery to tie off both tubes that carry urine from the kidneys. This was done to stop protein loss and help the body hold onto important fluids. After surgery, an imaging test showed mild fluid backup in the kidneys. During the 12-day hospital stay, the patient ate better and got stronger. The patient went home on long-term dialysis, which is a treatment that cleans the blood when kidneys cannot. The patient needed only a little help with walking.

Final Diagnoses:
Amyloidosis caused by an abnormal protein, with large protein loss in urine. The patient also has nerve damage that causes a big drop in blood pressure when standing up.

Procedures:
Surgery to tie off both tubes that carry urine from the kidneys. This was done through small cuts with a camera and hand assistance.

Follow-Up Plans:
The patient will see the kidney doctor for ongoing care of the kidney disease. Dialysis will continue as needed. More imaging tests may be done to check how the kidneys are working.

Blood tests showed the patient had low red blood cells and low cell counts that help with clotting. The patient's kidney function got worse, shown by rising waste products in his blood. The patient was diagnosed with Castleman's disease, a rare illness that affects many parts of the body. The patient also had high levels of a protein that affects blood vessel growth.

The patient received 10 blood filtering treatments to remove harmful substances from his blood. These treatments did not help his low blood cell counts or kidney problems. The patient then started cancer-fighting drugs called Rituximab, Etoposide, Cyclophosphamide, Vincristine, and Prednisone for 6 rounds. Within a week of starting these medicines, the patient's kidneys began working normally again. The patient's fever, belly fluid buildup, and swollen glands began to get better after starting treatment. The care team watched the patient closely during his hospital stay.

Hospital Course:
During the hospital stay, the patient's low red blood cells and clotting cell counts returned to normal. The patient's kidneys started working normally again. Blood tests that measure swelling in the body also returned to normal within the first few weeks. The patient stayed healthy for 2 years without needing any medicine.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient received full information about his illness and treatment choices. The patient was told to see his regular doctor and his specialty doctors for blood, cancer, and kidney care. The patient was told to get regular blood tests and imaging scans to check on his health.

The patient was sent home without any medications.

Hospital Course:
The patient was sent to our hospital because of frequent extra heartbeats coming from the lower heart chambers. Tests did not find any problems. A procedure was done to fix the irregular heartbeat using heat energy. After the procedure, the patient felt dizzy and had chest tightness, cold sweats, a slow heartbeat, and low blood pressure. More tests showed fluid had built up around the heart. A needle was used to drain 800 mL of blood from around the heart. The patient's chest tightness got better and blood pressure went up. But two hours later, the chest tightness came back. Another 750 mL of blood was drained through a tube left in place around the heart. The patient was given extra fluids and a medicine called dopamine to keep blood pressure normal. Over the next hour, the patient's blood flow became more unstable. An ultrasound of the heart showed a tear in the wall of the lower left heart chamber and a blood clot in that wall. The patient was then moved to the operating room for surgery.

Surgical intervention:
The patient had surgery where the chest was opened through the breastbone. A heart-lung machine was set up by placing tubes in the main blood vessel leaving the heart and the upper right heart chamber. This was done quickly after blood was removed from around the heart. The heart was stopped using a special solution. Looking at the heart showed a bruised area about 6 by 8 centimeters on the back and side wall. There was a 5-centimeter tear in the outer heart layer in the middle of this area. The tear was closed using stitches with supportive pads. A patch made from heart lining tissue was sewn around the bruised area with medical glue inside. The patient was taken off the heart-lung machine without problems. Blood was flowing well through the heart.

Discharge Summary:
The patient has healed well from the surgery and left the hospital 15 days after the operation. The final tests showed that the damaged area of the lower left heart chamber wall had healed.
